sentences: Okay, quick question.
Can one square be two colors at the same time?
Not a trick of the light.
Actually two colors, and both of them true.
Sounds fake, right?
Stick with me.
Back in the sixties, the artist Josef Albers showed that a color can look different depending on what's next to it.
But that's just your eyes.
Qontext goes way further.
In quantum physics, some things don't have one fixed answer.
What you get depends on how you check.
So here, a tile really is one color when you read it along its row, and a different color when you read it down its column.
Don't buy it?
Try Mermin's Dare.
Nine tiles, six rules.
Give every tile a plus or a minus and make all six rules happy.
You'll get five.
Everyone gets five.
A computer tried all five hundred and twelve ways.
Quantum gets six, every single time.
That's what the Qontext website runs on.
The second you open it, it rolls the dice and picks colors just for you.
That's your world.
Your friend gets a different one.
And colors you haven't scrolled to yet aren't decided.
They settle the moment you look.
Each room shows off a different trick.
Unity Wheel turns quantum math into perfect color combos.
Fringe mixes colors like waves of light.
Pentacle gives you five colors that never clash.
Spooky Pair links a light design and a dark one, so they react together.
And Unpaintables shows shapes you literally can't color by the rules.
Oh, and light mode versus dark mode?
Tap the moon.
You get a whole dial: light, dark, and every kind of dusk in between.
The text stays easy to read the whole way round.
Want to make something?
Open the Atelier, the studio.
Play with every room, pick your colors, and save your design as one short code you can share.
Bouncer works like a bouncer at a club: if your text is hard to read on any color, it's not getting in.
Handoff sends your colors to code and design tools, and Walk-By makes prints that change color as you walk past.
Got a website?
Drop in Observer.
It's one tiny file, and every visitor gets their own world.
No server, no tracking.
Designer?
Superpose puts the same grid in Figma, with a row version and a column version of every color.
Want the real deal?
Probe runs it all on an actual IBM quantum computer.
Then Notary checks the results and stamps them with a seal, so anyone can see exactly where your colors came from.
That's Qontext.
Colors that depend on how you look at them.
Open the Atelier and make your own world.
